title: The Paper Compass
premise: In 1918 London, Jonah Okonkwo, a Nigerian-born driver for suffragist Edith Vane, has quietly read and memorized the letters she delivers for two decades — letters that reveal a network of pacifists hiding deserters and forged papers. When a census taker named Ruth Calloway asks one question too many about a household that officially doesn't exist, Jonah must decide whether to protect Edith's secrets or trust Ruth with them. As armistice negotiations stall and government agents close in, Jonah smuggles the evidence — a ledger proving the network's innocence in a framed treason charge — past three checkpoints. She succeeds at devastating cost: Edith takes the fall publicly to save the others, Jonah inherits both the archive and the burden of truth, and years later she passes the paper compass — Edith's coded map of safe houses — to Ruth's daughter.
about_author: Quentin Marchetti is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in regional British record offices. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. During the 1918 census, Ruth Calloway notices the Vane house lists five residents but holds seven beds, and asks why. Jonah deflects with practiced ease but recognizes danger in Ruth's persistence. Emotional beat: the chill of a lifetime's careful silences cracking open.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Letters
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present: how young Jonah learned to read letters by lamplight before delivering them, and which ones she burned. Establishes her loyalty to Edith Vane and the code of protective silence. Emotional beat: tenderness entangled with deception.

chapters.title: The House That Doesn't Exist
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. We meet the hidden residents — a deserter, a forged-papers forger, a German-born nurse — and learn the network's purpose. Edith warns Jonah that the census taker must be handled. Emotional beat: fear sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Calloway Returns
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth files an anomaly report, then regrets it when she glimpses a frightened girl at the Vane window. Her own brother was shot as a deserter; her loyalty wavers between duty and memory. Emotional beat: guilt turning toward curiosity.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Jonah discovers Edith's hidden ledger documenting every person sheltered — proof they aided no treason, only conscience. But a government agent, Inspector Hale, is hunting the same book to frame the network for a sabotage it didn't commit. Emotional beat: hope shadowed by threat.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Post Office
chapters.summary: Jonah attempts to mail the ledger to a solicitor but finds the post office under watch. She memorizes instead, burning nothing yet, and realizes Hale has intercepted Edith's correspondence. Emotional beat: the trap tightening.

chapters.title: An Uneasy Alliance
chapters.summary: Ruth confronts Jonah directly; Jonah tests her with a false detail, and Ruth catches it — proving she thinks, not just reports. A fragile pact forms: Ruth will delay her report if Jonah shows her the truth. Emotional beat: distrust giving way to cautious alliance.

chapters.title: The Nurse's Testimony
chapters.summary: The German-born nurse, Greta, recounts the night of the sabotage she witnessed — men in uniforms who were not soldiers. Her account matches the ledger. POV alternates Greta and Jonah. Emotional beat: witness becoming weapon.

chapters.title: Hale Visits
chapters.summary: Inspector Hale calls at the Vane house, courteous and venomous, probing Edith about her 'charitable work.' Edith performs respectability brilliantly while Jonah hides the ledger beneath the floor of the coal cellar. Emotional beat: terror masked as tea and civility.

chapters.title: What Silences Cost
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, reflective midpoint. She reckons with twenty years of silences — the lovers separated, the dying denied last words — and questions whether protection has been kindness or cowardice. Emotional beat: moral reckoning.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: News spreads that an armistice may be signed within days; after that, deserters may be pardoned and the frame-up collapse — or be buried forever. The deadline crystallizes: evidence must move before the guns stop. Emotional beat: urgency like a drumbeat.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Network
chapters.summary: One resident, terrified, slips information to Hale in exchange for immunity. The deserter is nearly caught; the safe house is compromised. Jonah realizes checkpoints will now be manned specifically for her. Emotional beat: betrayal's bitter taste.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Railway
chapters.summary: Jonah carries the ledger sewn into her coat toward a contact at King's Cross, passing a document inspection through nerve and a borrowed wedding ring and widow's weeds. She reaches the contact — who is dead. Emotional beat: grief and improvisation.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ordered to identify Jonah from photographs, she refuses, destroying her own report and her career with it. She finds Jonah and offers herself fully to the cause. Emotional beat: sacrifice as self-discovery.

chapters.title: Edith Decides
chapters.summary: Edith reveals she has known about Jonah's letter-reading all along — and approves. She resolves to surrender herself publicly to draw Hale away from the ledger run, over Jonah's furious objection. Emotional beat: love expressed as letting go.

chapters.title: The Diversion
chapters.summary: Edith walks into a staged public arrest, buying hours. Hale, triumphant, pulls his men from the third checkpoint — almost. Jonah and Ruth slip toward the final obstacle with the ledger and Greta's sworn testimony. Emotional beat: heartbreak fueling momentum.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The Solicitor's Door
chapters.summary: The climax. One agent remains at the solicitor's chambers; Ruth creates a diversion that turns violent, and Jonah faces a choice: run with the ledger or go back for wounded Ruth. She does both — barely — as the documents reach the solicitor minutes before the armistice is announced. Emotional beat: everything risked, everything nearly lost.

chapters.title: The Guns Stop
chapters.summary: Church bells; crowds; the war over. The solicitor places the evidence before a magistrate. Hale's frame-up begins to unravel, but Edith remains in custody pending trial. Jonah stands in the celebrating streets unable to celebrate. Emotional beat: victory hollowed by cost.

chapters.title: Trial and Testimony
chapters.summary: Greta testifies; the dead contact's letters corroborate; Hale is discredited and the charges reframed. Edith is released to a crowd that once jeered her. Jonah watches from the back, unseen, as always. Emotional beat: justice arriving quiet and late.

chapters.title: Inheritance
chapters.summary: Edith, aging and weary, formally gives Jonah the archive — the ledger, the compass-map of safe houses, twenty years of letters — naming her its keeper. Jonah accepts not as a servant but as a successor. Emotional beat: inheritance as recognition.

chapters.title: The Paper Compass
chapters.summary: Years later, 1926. Jonah, now running the network quietly, meets Ruth's grown daughter and teaches her the codes, the routes, the reasons. The title object — Edith's hand-drawn map — changes hands. Emotional beat: continuity, purpose passed on.

chapters.title: Which Silences Keep People Safe
chapters.summary: Closing chapter, Jonah's voice. She writes her own letter at last — to Ruth, saying plainly what twenty years of reading others' letters taught her: that truth, carefully carried, is the only loyalty that lasts. She seals it and delivers it herself. Emotional beat: peace earned through speech.
